samples.summary: `openBrowser` is no longer wrapped in try/catch, so a rejection leaks the listening callback server and its 5-minute timer and later crashes on an unhandled rejection
samples.evidence: Before this change the call was `try { await deps.openBrowser(oauthUrl) } catch {}`. Now line 351 is a bare `await deps.openBrowser(armLaunch(oauthUrl));`. If that promise rejects, `runLogin` unwinds before `waitForCallback()`, so `close()` (the only `clearTimeout`/`srv.close()`) never runs: the http server keeps the event loop alive, and ~5 minutes later the armed timer calls `callbackReject(...)` on a `callbackPromise` nobody is awaiting — exactly the unhandled-rejection failure the comment at login.ts:786-794 was written to avoid. The shipped `openBrowser` swallows its own errors, so this fires only if the import/spawn path ever rejects outside that `try` or an injected dep rejects, hence low confidence — but the resource/timer leak on the error path is real.

samples.summary: Single-use launch link: any speculative or duplicate dereference (link scanner, opener probe, browser prefetch, second window) permanently breaks the login with no recovery inside the running command
samples.evidence: `armLaunch` parks the authorization URL and the handler sets `launchTarget = undefined` on the *first* GET of `/launch/<token>`, whoever makes it. The URL is handed to an arbitrary OS opener; a probe or prefetch that resolves it first leaves the real browser with the 410 page, and the running `wafflebase login` has no way to re-arm — it sits out the full 5-minute `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS` unless the user reads the page and Ctrl-Cs. Previously the authorization URL was idempotent, so a duplicate open was harmless. Re-arming on the same token (or arming a fresh one on demand) would keep the property without this failure mode.

samples.summary: Routing the browser through a loopback 302 may change `Sec-Fetch-Site` on the CLI start, which `GitHubAuthGuard.assertCliStartNotCrossSite` refuses with a 400
samples.evidence: The browser is now navigated to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<tok>` which 302s to `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli...` — a different site. `github-auth.guard.ts:309-319` throws `BadRequestException` for any CLI start whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is not `none`/`same-origin`/`same-site`. Previously the opener navigated straight to the backend, which is unambiguously `none`. Per Fetch Metadata the value stays `none` for a browser-initiated navigation even across redirects, so this probably holds — but if any shipping browser recomputes the header on the server redirect, every `wafflebase login` 400s. Nothing in the new tests exercises the header on the redirected request.

samples.summary: Half of the logout cookie sweep is inert: a `__Host-`-prefixed `Set-Cookie` without `Secure` is rejected by the browser, so the non-secure clears of the prefixed names can never take effect
samples.evidence: `clearAuthCookies` emits every name × `{secure:true,false}`. For `__Host-wafflebase_session` / `__Host-wafflebase_refresh` the `secure:false` variant violates the `__Host-` prefix rules and is discarded on arrival, so 2 of the 8 production Set-Cookie headers are dead and the doc comment's claim ("over http the one that can arrive does") does not hold for the prefixed names. Only the unprefixed pair actually benefits from the insecure variant.

samples.summary: `assertCliLoginAvailable()` runs before the port is parsed, so a `?mode=cli` request that is not even a usable CLI start now 400s instead of degrading to a browser login
samples.evidence: canActivate does `if (isCliStart) { assertCliStartNotCrossSite(req); assertCliLoginAvailable(); }` at lines 203-206, before `parseCliPort` at line 207. On a cleartext non-loopback deployment, `GET /auth/github?mode=cli` with a missing/invalid port throws BadRequestException, contradicting the middleware's own contract at cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:128-132 ("The guard ignores it too, so it falls through to an ordinary browser login rather than 404-ing here"). Moving the availability assert below the `port !== undefined` test would preserve the documented fall-through.

samples.summary: Two error emitters were left unattributed, so `ctx list` and `status` still print envelopes with no `command` while every sibling command now carries one
samples.evidence: `ctx.ts:85` and `status.ts:69` still call `outputError(e)` with no `Command` argument. `ctx list`'s NOT_LOGGED_IN envelope therefore lacks `command`, while the `ctx switch` path changed in this same diff emits `command: "ctx.switch"` — the exact per-subcommand inconsistency the change says it is removing.

samples.summary: `login-url.txt` is only removed in the `finally` around `waitForCallback`, so the recommended Ctrl-C recovery leaves the live login URL on disk
samples.evidence: The file written by `announceLoginUrl` (login.ts:157) is deleted only at login.ts:365. The spent-launch page the same change adds (SPENT_LAUNCH_PAGE, login.ts:493) instructs the user to "press Ctrl-C" — SIGINT terminates the process without running that `finally`, so the file holding the nonce + PKCE challenge survives the aborted login. No signal handler or `process.on('exit')` cleanup exists.

samples.summary: `process.exit(1)` immediately after `console.error(envelope)` can truncate the newly machine-readable envelope when stderr is a pipe
samples.evidence: ctx.ts:107-108 and 113-117 write the one-line envelope with `console.error` and then call `process.exit(1)`. On POSIX, writes to a pipe (the agent-harness case the envelope exists for) are asynchronous, so `process.exit` may drop the buffered line — leaving the consumer an exit code with no body. Setting `process.exitCode` and returning would avoid it.

finding.summary: `openBrowser` is no longer wrapped in try/catch, so a rejection leaks the listening callback server and its 5-minute timer and later crashes on an unhandled rejection
finding.evidence: Before this change the call was `try { await deps.openBrowser(oauthUrl) } catch {}`. Now line 351 is a bare `await deps.openBrowser(armLaunch(oauthUrl));`. If that promise rejects, `runLogin` unwinds before `waitForCallback()`, so `close()` (the only `clearTimeout`/`srv.close()`) never runs: the http server keeps the event loop alive, and ~5 minutes later the armed timer calls `callbackReject(...)` on a `callbackPromise` nobody is awaiting — exactly the unhandled-rejection failure the comment at login.ts:786-794 was written to avoid. The shipped `openBrowser` swallows its own errors, so this fires only if the import/spawn path ever rejects outside that `try` or an injected dep rejects, hence low confidence — but the resource/timer leak on the error path is real.

verdict.reason: The structural description is accurate — login.ts:351 is a bare `await deps.openBrowser(armLaunch(oauthUrl));`, `close()` (login.ts:822-825) runs only in the `finally` at login.ts:361-366, the 5-minute timer is armed earlier at login.ts:808-818, `callbackPromise` (login.ts:646-649) gets a handler only via `waitForCallback()`, and the top-level handler does not `process.exit()` for an unclassified throw (login.ts:48-60, 85; cli.ts:84-100). But the failure requires `deps.openBrowser` to reject, and it cannot. The production supplier is `openBrowser` (wired in `defaultLoginDeps`, login.ts:280-286), whose entire body — `await import('open')`, `await open(url)`, and the `child?.on?.('error')` attach — is inside one `try { ... } catch {}` with an empty catch (login.ts:118-126); no statement exists outside that try, so the promise resolves unconditionally. The reviewer's hypothesized "import/spawn path that rejects outside that try" does not exist in the code. The only other supplier of the dep is the test stub at packages/cli/test/login.test.ts:462, which resolves; grep found no other override. I also checked the other statements between server start (login.ts:320) and the try/finally (login.ts:359) — createPkcePair/encodeURIComponent, console.error (Node swallows console write errors), and announceLoginUrl whose filesystem work is itself wrapped (login.ts:151-171) — none supplies a real throw path. The leak/unhandled-rejection sequence is therefore unreachable on every existing path.

finding.summary: Single-use launch link: any speculative or duplicate dereference (link scanner, opener probe, browser prefetch, second window) permanently breaks the login with no recovery inside the running command
finding.evidence: `armLaunch` parks the authorization URL and the handler sets `launchTarget = undefined` on the *first* GET of `/launch/<token>`, whoever makes it. The URL is handed to an arbitrary OS opener; a probe or prefetch that resolves it first leaves the real browser with the 410 page, and the running `wafflebase login` has no way to re-arm — it sits out the full 5-minute `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS` unless the user reads the page and Ctrl-Cs. Previously the authorization URL was idempotent, so a duplicate open was harmless. Re-arming on the same token (or arming a fresh one on demand) would keep the property without this failure mode.

verdict.reason: The single-use launch mechanics are real (armLaunch at login.ts:826-830, launchTarget cleared at login.ts:663, 410 page at login.ts:681-689, no re-arm), but the finding's blocking impact claim — "permanently breaks the login with no recovery inside the running command ... sits out the full 5-minute CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS unless the user Ctrl-Cs" — is contradicted by the code one line later: runLogin calls announceLoginUrl(oauthUrl) unconditionally right after openBrowser (login.ts:351-355), which prints the actual authorization URL to a TTY stderr or writes it to a 0600 login-url.txt and prints the path (login.ts:141-172). The callback listener, nonce and PKCE pair are still live, so a launch link spent by a prefetch/probe is recoverable inside the same run by opening the announced authorization URL — no re-arm required. The worst residual case is following the 410 page's own explicit remedy (Ctrl-C, re-run; login.ts:490-495). That is a usability/design tradeoff, not a crash, data loss, dropped await, or broken invariant, so it is not blocking under the Correctness rubric. Behavior is also deliberate and covered by tests (packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:92-129).

finding.summary: Routing the browser through a loopback 302 may change `Sec-Fetch-Site` on the CLI start, which `GitHubAuthGuard.assertCliStartNotCrossSite` refuses with a 400
finding.evidence: The browser is now navigated to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/launch/<tok>` which 302s to `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli...` — a different site. `github-auth.guard.ts:309-319` throws `BadRequestException` for any CLI start whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is not `none`/`same-origin`/`same-site`. Previously the opener navigated straight to the backend, which is unambiguously `none`. Per Fetch Metadata the value stays `none` for a browser-initiated navigation even across redirects, so this probably holds — but if any shipping browser recomputes the header on the server redirect, every `wafflebase login` 400s. Nothing in the new tests exercises the header on the redirected request.

verdict.reason: The launch-redirect code and the Sec-Fetch-Site check both exist as quoted, but the claimed breakage ("every `wafflebase login` 400s") is unreachable. `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware` is applied to `GET auth/github` (auth.module.ts:45-48) and runs before `GitHubAuthGuard`; the navigation produced by the loopback 302 carries no `confirm` param and no matching confirm cookie, so the middleware sends the 200 confirmation page at cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:162-171 and never calls `next()`. `assertCliStartNotCrossSite` (github-auth.guard.ts:309-319, called at :204) therefore never runs on the redirected request; the only request that reaches it is the same-origin "Continue" click on the backend's own page (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:197,234), which is in ALLOWED_FETCH_SITES (:129). Even under the reviewer's own hypothetical of a browser recomputing the header across the redirect (which the reviewer concedes the Fetch Metadata spec forbids for a browser-initiated navigation), the user gets the confirmation page rather than a 400. The two fall-through paths that do reach the guard on the first request are `!cliLoginAvailable()` (middleware :121-123), where the CLI login is already refused unconditionally by assertCliLoginAvailable (guard :239-252), and `port === undefined` (middleware :128-132), which an ephemeral `srv.listen(0)` port cannot produce given parseCliPort's >=1024 floor (guard :149-154).

mergedFrom.summary: `openBrowser` attaches the child `error` listener too late to catch a failed spawn

finding.summary: `openBrowser` attaches the child `error` listener after `await`, which may be too late to prevent an uncaught exception

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as quoted: packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:121-122 does `const child = await open(url); child?.on?.('error', () => {});`, installing the child 'error' listener only in a post-await microtask. Whether that is too late depends solely on open@11.0.0's internals: the source comment at login.ts:105-109 asserts open attaches `once('error', reject)` synchronously with the spawn and resolves on 'spawn' (which would turn ENOENT into a caught rejection), while the finding asserts open v11 returns the subprocess with no listener (which would let the nextTick-scheduled 'error' fire before the listener is attached, crashing the CLI mid-login on a headless box). pnpm-lock.yaml:322-324 pins open@11.0.0 but no copy is installed or vendored in this tree (no matches for **/node_modules/open/**), so I could not read the `subprocess` block to settle it. The reviewer's claim about the test is verified and accurate: login-callback.test.ts:21 mocks the entire 'open' module, and the absorption test at lines 177-186 emits 'error' on a hand-built EventEmitter after openBrowser has already returned, so the real spawn/nextTick ordering is never exercised and the test cannot detect the bug. No refutation ground applies: the code is present as described, the only candidate guard lives inside the unreadable dependency, and an unhandled 'error' event crashing the login flow is squarely in the correctness lane (critical impact if real). Unresolved uncertainty keeps the finding.
